name: Johan Irving Søltoft
bio: Johan Irving Søltoft is a Postdoctoral Researcher in the Section for Science and Technology Studies. His research is driven by a methodological ambition to develop new ways of giving voice to perspectives that are divergent and often excluded or muted in bureaucratic processes. This work explores new approaches to bringing such perspectives into interaction with AI and synthetic ethnography.

name: Benjamin Lipp
bio: Benjamin Lipp is Assistant Professor at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU). He received his PhD in Science and Technology Studies (STS) from the Technical University of Munich in 2019. Before joining DTU in 2023, he was a Marie Curie Postdoctoral Fellow at Cornell University and the University of Hamburg. His work draws on STS, sociology, and media studies to investigate and theorise the techno-political conditions under which machines and people interface. His research covers emerging technologies especially in healthcare, from robotics and neurotechnology to artificial intelligence. Informed by a co-creative approach, Benjamin has been innovating formats for teaching Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) in STEM education.
quotes: The unthinkable thought is not to disagree that we are like machines but to imagine a human future without them - Katherine Hayles in Computing the human, 2003

name: Anders Kristian Munk
bio: I am Professor of Computational Anthropology and head of ECHOlab at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU). My research focuses on controversies around a wide range of sociotechnical problems, spanning from energy and climate change to food systems, urban planning, and artificial intelligence. I develop computationally assisted methods for controversy mapping, combining ethnographic and participatory approaches with large scale qualitative data analysis, machine learning and natural language processing.

name: William Vergo
bio: I'm a Danish engineer pursuing a PhD at the Technical University of Denmark. Building on my engineering background and my experience as a public servant in the Danish Energy Agency, my expertise lies in energy modeling, policy, and regulation, and I thrive at the intersection of technology, policy, and societal needs. My primary research goal is to improve methods for co-production of techno-economic data regarding energy systems. The main research object in this regard is the Danish Energy Agency's "Technology Catalogues," which compile cost and performance data for a wide range of energy technologies and are internationally referenced in modeling and policy.

name: Brit Ross Winthereik
bio: Brit Ross Winthereik is Professor and Head of Division. Her research focuses on digitalization processes, infrastructure development, and the use of data for management and governance in the public sector. Her methodological outlook is ethnographic, and she develops experimental research methods and material-based analytics. Her co-authored and edited volumes include 'Monitoring Movements in Development Aid: Recursive Infrastructures and Partnerships' (MIT Press, 2013), ‘Electrifying Anthropology’ (Bloomsberry, 2019), 'Experimenting with Ethnography' (Duke University Press, 2021), and 'Handbook for the Anthropology of Technology' (Palgrave Handbook Series, 2021), and ‘Energy Worlds in Experiment’ (Mattering Press, 2021). She is an avid contributor to the public media discourse.

name: Tanja Schneider
bio: Tanja Schneider is Head of the Science and Technology Studies Section at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and Associate Professor of Science and Technology Studies (STS). She is also Research Affiliate at the Institute for Science, Innovation & Society (InSIS) in the Department of Anthropology at the University of Oxford and Associated Member of the STS Lab at the University of Lausanne. Tanja's research is rooted in science and technology studies (STS) and builds bridges to adjacent fields including the anthropology and sociology of food, health, markets, consumption, and digital sociology. Over time, her work has developed along three interrelated strands: 1) emergence of new research fields and communities, 2) digital technologies, everyday life, and ethical consumption, and 3) valuation studies and the valuing of sustainability.

name: Julius Kob
bio: Julius is a postdoc in the Expertise of Expectations project of Julia Kirch Kirkegaard. He is an economic sociologist exploring knowledge and valuation at the intersection of economy and nature with a focus on financial knowledge production and epistemic authority in technoscience and socioecological crisis. In his PhD in sociology at the University of Edinburgh, Julius explored the financialisaton of disasters in a study on natural catastrophe modelling and its emergence and design in (re)insurance and capital markets. As a research fellow at Warwick Business School, he then co-developed and conducted a 4-year, team-ethnographic study on climate-related knowledge production and use in the institutional investment industry. With a background in sociology, social studies of finance and STS, he holds an Honorary Fellowship at the University of Warwick, a master in sociology from the London School of Economics, and has been a visiting researcher at The New School and at Columbia University and a teaching fellow at Hamburg University
quotes: It is the heuristic nature of processes of knowledge production that, if increasingly enclosed in proprietary settings, concentrate and privatise authority in knowing socioecological relations and in the discretion over its distribution. Its successful deployment can entitle to wield broader epistemic power in technoscientific and financialising ecological emergency.;Inherent in the multitude of measures around green finance is the claim by parts of the financial sector to the authority of being a legitimate and competent governor of the planet’s climate. It is this inherent claim in the anchoring of finance into the intergovernmental, transnational, and domestic attempts to govern climate-society relations that compel us to understand green finance as financial climate governance. This claim to govern by financial means, i.e. through the mechanisms, paradigms, and practices of modern finance, appears as quasi-naturalised and, thus, often remains implicit. The position of power which finance occupies in financialised capitalism at large, seems to imbue the financial sector with the entitlement to claim the authority, competence, and responsibility to further wield said power – seemingly for the good of the planet.

name: Frederik Bay-Jørgensen
bio: I am a PhD fellow and part of the project Culturally Explainable AI (CXAI), which aims to develop theory and methods for studying generative AI and AI alignment from an anthropological perspective.
quotes: The individual mind is immanent but not only in the body. It is immanent also in pathways and messages outside the body, and there is a larger Mind of which the individual mind is only a sub-system. - Gregory Bateson, Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972)

name: Csilla Duray
bio: I am a PhD student at the STS Section with a background in Social Data Science, Urban Planning and Public Policy. I am interested in how digital traces and algorithms can help us understand human lived experiences and non-human behaviour in urban environments. Within this context, I am currently exploring how the use of generative AI tools can support or hinder citizen engagement. Specifically, I study how people experience public transport as part of the Horizon Europe-funded MOVEO project, and how these insights can be communicated to planners.
quotes: Models are not complete until reviewed by the people described in them. - Sarah Williams in Data Action, 2020;Still there are seeds to be gathered, and room in the bag of stars. - Ursula K. Le Guin in The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction, 1986

name: Anders Koed Madsen
bio: Anders Koed Madsen is Professor of Data, Democracy, and Digital Urbanism at the STS section at Technical University of Denmark. His research examines how machine learning applied to large-scale qualitative data can inform policy-making and urban planning. Including how different data infrastuctures afford specific ways of valueing and governing cities. Under the concept of Soft City Sensing, he has collaborated with urban design firms such as Gehl, Henning Larsen, and BIG.

name: Daniel Nordstrand Frantzen
bio: I'm a sociologist occupied with valuations, justifications, and critique in controversies of technology. Most of my work has so far considered issues relating to the planning and development of wind farms locally.

name: Rebekka Nordal
bio: I am a PhD student in STS section at DTU Man, where I explore how networks of concerned actors within institutions of expertise and in civil society propose alternative expectations to how the future of green hydrogen could and should be devised for a socio-technically sustainable energy transition. With a BA and MSc in Sociology from University of Copenhagen, I hold an interest in the intersection between STS and sociology of knowledge, with a focus on environmental and energy-related issues.

name: Emil Nissen
bio: Based in wind energy studies, I use my educational background in techno-anthropology and human ecology to explore the transition to renewable energy technologies, inquiring who benefits from current modes of transitioning

name: Tais Abrahamsson
bio: My background is in sustainable energy design and electrical engineering, but my real interest is in how renewable energy may be used as a medium for developing both social and environmental sustainability.

name: David Westergren Broomham
bio: David Broomham is a PhD Fellow at DTU, developing the Urban Listening Toolkit as part of the EU-funded CULTIGEN project. With a Masters in Social Data Science, he builds tools for listening to digital publics and visualising diverse urban perspectives, developing approaches on how to do qualitative research at scale.

name: Mathieu Jacomy
bio: Mathieu Jacomy is Doctor of Techno-Anthropology and research engineer at DTU (Technical University of Denmark). He has been assistant professor at the Techno-Anthropology Lab and a research engineer for 10 years at the Sciences Po médialab in Paris. He is a co-founder of Gephi, a popular open source network visualization tool. He develops digital instruments involving data visualization and network analysis for the social science and humanities. He has been co-organizing the Open Research devroom since its inception in 2020. His research has notably focused on the practices of user communities around open source tools in the social sciences and humanities. With Gephi, he received the Java Duke award in 2010 and the ICWSM conference Test of Time Award in 2019. He writes about digital instruments and complexity on https://reticular.hypotheses.org and toots at @jacomyma@mas.to.

name: Amanda Obitz Mogensen
bio: My research focuses on how financial actors participate in constructing and legitimizing the infrastructures and claims that contemporary societies come to depend on. My research sits at the intersection of STS and anthropology. I study who has agency over financial decisions and how do these decisions transform infrastructures, landscapes, and everyday experiences across different empirical settings, so far my research have been on pension finance and hyperscale data centres.
quotes: Instead of taking capitalism a priori, as an already determining structure, logic, and trajectory, we ask how its social relations are generated out of divergent life projects. name: Amelie Lange
bio: Amelie is a PhD student at the STS section. She is an STS scholar and ethnographer with a background in anthropology. Throughout her PhD on the automation of chronic pain care, she has developed a fascination with the sociology of scoring, with the histories of measuring the body and the work that numbers do in practice (particularly in the clinic). Say hi if you want to chat about temporality and explore the concept of the "chronic" together, or discuss the diverse politics of datafying chronic illness.
